topic: Reciprocating engine induction and cooling systems

notes.front: In an aircraft reciprocating engine, what does the basic induction system consist of?
notes.back: An air scoop that collects the inlet air and ducting that carries that air to the inlet filter.
notes.explanation: The filter is generally housed in the carburettor heat box or a nearby housing attached to the carburettor or fuel injection controller.
notes.example: Like the air intake and hose on a car engine, but fed from a scoop in the engine cowling.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Induction Systems”, p. 3-1
notes.evidence: The basic induction system of an aircraft reciprocating engine consists of an air scoop used to collect the inlet air and ducting that transfers the air to the inlet filter. The air filter is generally housed in the carburetor heat box or other housing close by

notes.front: What is carburettor heat?
notes.back: An alternate warm air source, selected by a valve below the carburettor, used to prevent carburettor icing.
notes.explanation: The heat valve admits outside air from the scoop in normal operation and warm engine-compartment air in icing conditions.
notes.example: Like switching a heater intake from outside air to air warmed around the exhaust, pulled by a push-pull knob in the flight deck.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Basic Carburetor Induction System”, p. 3-1
notes.evidence: A carburetor heat air valve is located below the carburetor for selecting an alternate warm air source (carburetor heat) to prevent carburetor icing.

notes.front: What does an alternate air valve (alternate air door) do in an induction system?
notes.back: It is spring-loaded closed and is sucked open by engine suction if the normal airflow route becomes blocked.
notes.explanation: No pilot action is needed: engine suction alone opens it when the normal route is blocked.
notes.example: Like a spring-loaded flap that pops open on its own when the main air path is choked, with no pilot action.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Basic Carburetor Induction System”, p. 3-1
notes.evidence: An alternate air door can be opened by engine suction if the normal route of airflow should be blocked by something. The valve is spring loaded closed and is sucked open by the engine if needed.

notes.front: What is the job of the induction air filter?
notes.back: To stop dust and other foreign matter from entering the engine through the carburettor.
notes.explanation: The filter sits in the air scoop in front of the carburettor air duct, and filtered air then enters the fuel metering device.
notes.example: Like a vacuum cleaner’s filter, but in paper, foam or oiled screen, and serviced at set intervals.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Basic Carburetor Induction System”, p. 3-1
notes.evidence: The carburetor air filter, shown in Figure 3-6, is installed in the air scoop in front of the carburetor air duct. Its purpose is

notes.front: What is a supercharger?
notes.back: An air compressor that raises the pressure of the air taken into the cylinders of a reciprocating engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook classifies supercharging systems as internally driven or externally driven (turbosupercharged).
notes.example: Like a pump that force-feeds air into the intake, whether driven by gears from the engine or by an exhaust turbine.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Supercharger. An air compressor used to increase the pressure of the air being taken into the cylinders of a reciprocating engine.

notes.front: What is an internally driven supercharger?
notes.back: A supercharger driven by the engine through a mechanical connection, compressing the air-fuel mixture after it leaves the carburettor.
notes.explanation: The handbook says these were used almost exclusively in high-horsepower radial engines.
notes.example: Like a fan geared to the crankshaft behind the carburettor, as on large radial engines in some cargo and spray planes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Internally Driven Superchargers”, p. 3-6
notes.evidence: Internally-driven superchargers were used almost exclusively in high horsepower radial reciprocating engines and are engine driven through a mechanical connection.

notes.front: What is a turbocharger?
notes.back: An exhaust-driven air compressor: a small radial inflow turbine in the exhaust drives a centrifugal compressor on the same shaft.
notes.explanation: The compressed air goes to the cylinders to increase the power of the reciprocating engine.
notes.example: Like the internally driven supercharger, but powered by exhaust gas that would otherwise go overboard.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Turbocharger. An exhaust-driven air compressor used to increase the power of a reciprocating engine. A turbocharger uses a small radial inflow turbine in the exhaust system to drive a centrifugal-type air compressor on the turbine shaft.

notes.front: What is a normalising turbocharger system?
notes.back: An exhaust-driven system that makes up the power lost to lower pressure at altitude, without boosting manifold pressure above 30 "Hg.
notes.explanation: Because it never goes above 30 "Hg, the handbook says it was not designed as a true supercharger.
notes.example: Like topping a tyre back up to its normal pressure, never beyond it, as the aircraft climbs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Normalizer Turbocharger”, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: These systems were not designed to be used as a true supercharger (boost manifold pressure over 30 "Hg). They compensate for the power lost due to the pressure drop resulting from increased altitude.

notes.front: What is a ground-boosted (sea level-boosted) turbocharger system?
notes.back: A turbosupercharger that works from sea level up to critical altitude, raising manifold pressure above 30 "Hg.
notes.explanation: Engines so fitted can develop more power at sea level than an engine without turbosupercharging.
notes.example: Like the normalising turbocharger, but already pushing extra pressure into the engine on the take-off roll.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Ground-Boosted Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: Some ground-boosted (sea level) turbosupercharged systems are designed to operate from sea level up to their critical altitude. These engines, sometimes referred to as sea level-boosted engines, can develop more power at sea level than an engine without turbosupercharging.

notes.front: What is a waste gate?
notes.back: A controllable butterfly valve in the exhaust of a turbocharged engine: open, exhaust leaves through the pipe; closed, it goes through the turbine.
notes.explanation: By choosing how much exhaust reaches the turbine, it sets the rotor speed and so the boost.
notes.example: Like a bypass door beside a water wheel: shut it and all the flow turns the wheel; open it and the wheel slows.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Waste gate. A controllable butterfly valve in the exhaust pipe of a reciprocating engine equipped with an exhaust-driven turbocharger. When the waste gate is open, exhaust gases leave the engine through the exhaust pipe, and when it is closed, they leave through the turbine.

notes.front: What is critical altitude?
notes.back: The maximum altitude at which, in standard atmosphere, a specified power or manifold pressure can be kept at a specified rotational speed.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that a critical altitude exists for every possible power setting below the maximum operating ceiling.
notes.example: Like the highest floor a pump can still lift water to at full pressure; above it, pressure starts to fall.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-12
notes.evidence: Critical altitude means the maximum altitude at which, in standard atmosphere, it is possible to maintain, at a specified rotational speed, a specified power or a specified manifold pressure. A critical altitude exists for every possible power setting below the maximum operating ceiling.

notes.front: What is an overboost condition?
notes.back: A condition in which manifold pressure exceeds the limits prescribed for the engine; it can cause serious damage.
notes.explanation: Some systems carry a pressure relief valve, set slightly above maximum deck pressure, to prevent damaging overboost if the system malfunctions.
notes.example: Like over-inflating a tyre beyond its rated pressure, rather than merely a gauge that wanders.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-14
notes.evidence: An overboost condition is one in which manifold pressure exceeds the limits prescribed for a particular engine and can cause serious damage. A pressure relief valve when used in some systems, set slightly in excess of maximum deck pressure, is provided to prevent damaging over boost in the event of a system malfunction.

notes.front: What is a variable absolute pressure controller (VAPC)?
notes.back: A turbocharger controller whose required upper deck pressure is scheduled by throttle position through a throttle-driven cam on an aneroid.
notes.explanation: As the throttle opens, the cam presses harder on the aneroid, so more deck pressure is needed to open the oil restrictor valve.
notes.example: Like a thermostat whose set point is moved by the throttle lever: open the throttle and the target deck pressure rises.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Variable Absolute Pressure Controller (VAPC)”, p. 3-15
notes.evidence: This means that the scheduled absolute value of upper deck pressure that is required to overcome the aneroid is variable by throttle position.

notes.front: What is a sloped controller?
notes.back: A turbocharger controller that keeps rated compressor discharge pressure at wide-open throttle and reduces it at part throttle.
notes.explanation: It senses both deck pressure and the pressure difference across the throttle, and responds more to that difference.
notes.example: Like a governor that gives full boost with the lever fully forward and eases boost off as the lever comes back.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Sloped Controller”, p. 3-15
notes.evidence: The sloped controller is designed to maintain the rated compressor discharge pressure at wide-open throttle and to reduce this pressure at part throttle settings.

notes.front: What is an absolute pressure controller?
notes.back: A turbocharger controller, with an aneroid referenced to upper deck pressure, that controls the system only at maximum output.
notes.explanation: When its set absolute pressure is reached it bypasses oil, relieving pressure on the waste gate actuator and so limiting compressor discharge pressure.
notes.example: Like a pressure-relief ceiling: it does nothing until deck pressure reaches its set value, then holds it there.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Absolute Pressure Controller”, p. 3-15
notes.evidence: One device used to control the speed and output of the turbocharger, but controls the system only at maximum output, is the absolute pressure controller. The absolute pressure controller contains an aneroid bellows that is referenced to upper deck pressure.

notes.front: What is an intercooler?
notes.back: An air-to-air heat exchanger between a turbosupercharger and the carburettor that cools the compressed air to prevent detonation.
notes.explanation: Compressing air heats it, so cooling it before it reaches the cylinders keeps the charge further from detonation.
notes.example: Like a small radiator for the intake air, placed after the compressor and before the throttle.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Intercooler. An air-to-air heat exchanger installed between a turbosupercharger and the carburetor. Intercoolers decrease the temperature of compressed air to prevent detonation.

notes.front: What does a reciprocating engine’s cooling system usually consist of?
notes.back: The engine cowling, cylinder baffles and cylinder fins, with cowl flaps on some engines.
notes.explanation: Temperature-indicating systems such as cylinder head, oil and exhaust gas temperature are also part of the picture.
notes.example: Like the fins on a motorcycle cylinder, but boxed in by cowling and baffles so the airflow is forced where it is needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling System Maintenance”, p. 6-34
notes.evidence: The engine cooling system of most reciprocating engines usually consists of the engine cowling, cylinder baffles, cylinder fins, and some use a type of cowl flaps.

notes.front: What are cowl flaps?
notes.back: Flaps at the cowling exit, moved by electric jackscrews, hydraulic actuators or by hand, that are the most common way to control cooling.
notes.explanation: Opening them increases cooling but adds drag, so they trade streamlining for cooling.
notes.example: Like adjustable louvres at the back of a radiator grille, opened on a hot day in traffic and closed on the motorway.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-33
notes.evidence: The most common means of controlling cooling is the use of cowl flaps. [Figure 6-51] These flaps are opened and closed by electric motor-driven jackscrews, by hydraulic actuators, or manually in some light aircraft.

notes.front: What is augmenter (augmentor) cooling?
notes.back: Using exhaust gas flowing through augmentor tubes to create low pressure that draws extra cooling air over the engine.
notes.explanation: Because exhaust gas velocity drives the airflow, cooling does not depend entirely on the propeller slipstream.
notes.example: Like a chimney whose rising hot gas pulls fresh air in through the room behind it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-33
notes.evidence: This low-pressure area in the augmentors draws additional cooling air over the engine. Air entering the outer shells of the augmentors is heated through contact with the augmentor tubes but is not contaminated with exhaust gases.

notes.front: What is a baffle in an air-cooled reciprocating engine?
notes.back: A thin sheet-metal shroud or bulkhead that directs cooling air between and around the cylinder fins.
notes.explanation: Baffles keep the air close around the cylinders instead of letting it rush past unused.
notes.example: Like the plastic ducting inside a computer case that forces fan air across the processor’s heat sink.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: Baffle. A thin sheet metal shroud or bulkhead used to direct the flow of cooling air between and around the cylinder fins of an air-cooled reciprocating engine.

notes.front: What does a cylinder temperature indicating system usually consist of?
notes.back: An indicator, electrical wiring and a thermocouple.
notes.explanation: The wiring runs from the instrument to the nacelle firewall, where it joins the thermocouple leads that go to the cylinder.
notes.example: Like a meat thermometer wired to a dial in the kitchen, but probing the hottest cylinder head.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: This system usually consists of an indicator, electrical wiring, and a thermocouple. The wiring is between the instrument and the nacelle firewall.

notes.front: How does a liquid-cooled reciprocating engine get rid of its heat?
notes.back: Coolant circulates through water jackets around the cylinders, and a heat exchanger or radiator then dissipates the heat into airflow.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that some diesel liquid-cooled engines are now available for light aircraft, though most are air cooled.
notes.example: Like a car engine’s radiator system, carried on an aircraft that must also lift the weight of the coolant.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-32
notes.evidence: In a liquid-cooled engine, around the cylinder are water jackets, in which liquid coolant is circulated and the coolant takes away the excess heat. The excess heat is then dissipated by a heat exchanger or radiator using air flow.

notes.front: How does the Rotax 912/914 cooling system cool the engine?
notes.back: Liquid cooling of the cylinder heads and ram-air cooling of the cylinders.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes it under the Rotax 912/914 heading using the Rotax 914’s system.
notes.example: Like an air-cooled engine with a small car-type coolant loop added just for the hot cylinder heads.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Rotax 912/914: Cooling System”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: The cooling system of the Rotax 914, shown in Figure 11-7, is designed for liquid cooling of the cylinder heads and ram-air cooling of the cylinders.

notes.front: What two air-cooling versions are available for the Rotax 447 and 503 two-stroke engines?
notes.back: Free air-cooling, from aircraft speed and propeller, and fan cooling, from a crankshaft-driven fan.
notes.explanation: The fan is driven permanently from the crankshaft through a V-belt.
notes.example: Like the difference between a bicycle-mounted lamp cooled by riding and a desk lamp with its own fan.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Cooling System of Rotax 447 UL SCDI & Rotax 503 UL DCDI”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: The first method is free air-cooling, which is a process of engine cooling by an air-stream generated by aircraft speed

notes.front: On the Rotax 914, what does the turbo control unit (TCU) do?
notes.back: It controls boost electronically through the waste gate, using throttle position, and drives a red boost lamp and orange caution lamp.
notes.explanation: The waste gate regulates turbocharger speed and so the boost pressure in the airbox.
notes.example: Like the oil-pressure controllers of larger turbocharged engines, but electronic, with warning lamps for the pilot.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Turbocharger & Control System”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: The turbo control unit (TCU) is furnished with output connections for an external red boost lamp and an orange caution lamp for indications of the functioning of the TCU.

notes.front: The air coming out of the throttle is called manifold pressure; it is measured in {{c1::inches of mercury ("Hg)}} and controls engine power output.
notes.explanation: The throttle plate controls how much air reaches the engine, and that pressure is what the manifold pressure gauge reads.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Induction Systems”, p. 3-1
notes.evidence: The air coming out of the throttle is referred to as manifold pressure. This pressure is measured in inches of mercury ("Hg) and controls engine power output.

notes.front: Why is induction system icing an operating hazard?
notes.back: It can cut off the flow of the air-fuel charge or vary the air-fuel ratio.
notes.explanation: Ice can form in cloud, fog, rain, sleet, snow, or even clear air with high humidity.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-3
notes.evidence: Induction system icing is an operating hazard because it can cut off the flow of the air-fuel charge or vary the air-fuel ratio. Ice can form in the induction system while an aircraft is flying in clouds, fog, rain, sleet, snow, or even clear air that has high moisture content (high humidity).

notes.front: An engine ran perfectly on the ground after an inspection, but the pilot reports it ran roughly and lost power in humid air in flight. What does the handbook say to consider?
notes.back: A) Induction system ice, which can cause such trouble in the air even when all checks pass
notes.choices:
A) Induction system ice, which can cause such trouble in the air even when all checks pass
B) Only a magneto fault, since icing needs visible moisture
C) Nothing: a good ground run rules out induction trouble
D) Only fuel contamination, since ice cannot form in clear air
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: a perfect ground run does not rule out icing in flight. B and D are wrong: ice can form even in clear air with high humidity.
notes.explanation: The handbook says many engine troubles blamed on other sources are actually caused by induction system icing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-3
notes.evidence: Even when an inspection shows that everything is in proper working order and the engine performs perfectly on the ground, induction system ice can cause an engine to act erratically and lose power in the air.

notes.front: Which type of induction ice forms because evaporating fuel lowers the air temperature?
notes.back: Fuel evaporation ice, also called refrigeration ice.
notes.explanation: It frequently occurs where fuel is injected upstream of the throttle, as in float-type carburettors.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 2, Engine Fuel & Fuel Metering Systems, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 2-8
notes.evidence: Fuel evaporation ice or refrigeration ice is formed because of the decrease in air temperature resulting from the evaporation of fuel after it is introduced into the airstream.

notes.front: Which type of induction ice forms on the rear side of a partly closed throttle?
notes.back: Throttle ice.
notes.explanation: Air rushing past the throttle valve creates low pressure behind it, cooling the charge so moisture freezes there.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 2, Engine Fuel & Fuel Metering Systems, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 2-9
notes.evidence: Throttle ice is formed on the rear side of the throttle, usually when the throttle is in a partially “closed” position. The rush of air across and around the throttle valve causes a low pressure on the rear side

notes.front: Which type of induction ice collects where the airflow changes direction, such as on the carburettor elbow or screen?
notes.back: Impact ice.
notes.explanation: It forms from snow, sleet or liquid water striking surfaces below 32 °F; on the carburettor screen it can cut airflow and power very quickly.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 2, Engine Fuel & Fuel Metering Systems, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 2-9
notes.evidence: Because of inertia effects, impact ice collects on or near a surface that changes the direction of the airflow. This type of ice may build up on the carburetor elbow, as well as the carburetor screen and metering elements.

notes.front: Why does applying carburettor heat cause a noticeable loss of power?
notes.back: Heated air expands and loses density, so a lighter charge reaches the cylinders and volumetric efficiency falls.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns that careless use of carburettor heat can be as dangerous as advanced induction icing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-3
notes.evidence: Increasing the temperature of the air causes it to expand and decrease in density. This action reduces the weight of the charge delivered to the cylinder and causes a noticeable loss in power because of decreased volumetric efficiency.

notes.front: If carburettor heat is applied with no icing present and the throttle setting unchanged, the mixture becomes {{c1::richer}}.
notes.explanation: The same passage warns that high intake air temperature may also cause detonation, especially during take-off and high-power operation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-3
notes.evidence: If icing is not present when carburetor heat or induction system anti-icing is applied and the throttle setting does not change, the mixture will become richer. In addition, high intake air temperature may cause detonation and engine failure, especially during takeoff and high power operation.

notes.front: A mechanic is about to start an engine for a ground run. The carburettor heat control is in the hot position. What should be done?
notes.back: D) Select cold: heat should not be used while starting, to protect the heater valves if the engine backfires
notes.choices:
A) Select hot only if outside air is below freezing
B) Leave it hot: warm air helps the fuel vaporise during the start
C) Leave it hot, then use full heat throughout the ground run
D) Select cold: heat should not be used while starting, to protect the heater valves if the engine backfires
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: heat should not be used during the start, and on the ground only enough for smooth running. A is wrong: the handbook gives no temperature exception for starting.
notes.explanation: During ground running afterwards, only enough carburettor heat to give smooth operation should be used.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: To prevent damage to the heater valves in the case of backfire, carburetor heat should not be used while starting the engine. Also, during ground operation only enough carburetor heat should be used to give smooth engine operation.

notes.front: An aircraft is flying through dry snow, with no sign of induction icing. Where does the handbook say the carburettor heat control is best left?
notes.back: A) In the cold position
notes.choices:
A) In the cold position
B) Partly hot, to keep the snow soft
C) Alternating hot and cold every few minutes
D) Full hot, to stop the snow entering
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are wrong: heat may melt the snow, and the water can refreeze on the induction walls.
notes.explanation: Heat could melt the snow, and the moisture could then collect and freeze on the induction system walls.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: It is best to leave the control in this position if there are particles of dry snow or ice in the air. The use of heat may melt the ice or snow, and the resulting moisture may collect and freeze on the walls of the induction system.

notes.front: What is the best way to remove throttle ice, or any ice that restricts airflow or lowers manifold pressure?
notes.back: Full carburettor heat.
notes.explanation: If there is enough heat and it is not applied late, the handbook says the ice clears in a few minutes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Icing”, p. 3-3
notes.evidence: Throttle ice or any ice that restricts airflow or reduces manifold pressure can best be removed by using full carburetor heat.

notes.front: How does dust drawn into the cylinders wear an engine?
notes.back: It grinds down cylinder walls and piston rings, then contaminates the oil and wears bearings and gears.
notes.explanation: In extreme cases an accumulation may clog an oil passage and starve the engine of oil.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Filtering”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: It acts on the cylinder walls by grinding down these surfaces and the piston rings. Then, it contaminates the oil and is carried through the engine, causing further wear on the bearings and gears. In extreme cases, an accumulation may clog an oil passage and cause oil starvation.

notes.front: What does dust do if it collects on the carburettor’s fuel-metering elements?
notes.back: It upsets the proper relation between airflow and fuel flow at all engine power settings.
notes.explanation: Dust is hard, abrasive particles carried by the air, so it harms metering as well as wearing surfaces.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Filtering”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: It can also collect on the fuel-metering elements of the carburetor, upsetting the proper relation between airflow and fuel flow at all engine power settings.

notes.front: Why do some filter installations have a spring-loaded filter door?
notes.back: It opens automatically when the filter is excessively restricted, so a clogged filter does not cut off airflow.
notes.explanation: A filter can clog with ice or dirt, for example after becoming rain-soaked and freezing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Filtering”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: Some installations have a spring-loaded filter door which automatically opens when the filter is excessively restricted. This prevents the airflow from being cut off when the filter is clogged with ice or dirt.

notes.front: During all regularly scheduled engine inspections, what should the induction system be checked for?
notes.back: Cracks and leaks, and security of mounting of its units.
notes.explanation: The system should also be kept clean, as stray material can restrict airflow.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: The induction system should be checked for cracks and leaks during all regularly scheduled engine inspections. The units of the system should be checked for security of mounting.

notes.front: After refitting an induction air duct, a mechanic cannot account for a shop rag and one of the duct clamp nuts. What is the concern before the engine is run?
notes.back: D) The rag could restrict airflow and the loose nut could seriously damage the engine
notes.choices:
A) None: the air filter will stop both items
B) Only the rag matters, since metal parts pass harmlessly through
C) Only the nut matters, since cloth burns away
D) The rag could restrict airflow and the loose nut could seriously damage the engine
notes.choicesExplained: A assumes the item is upstream of the filter, which may not be so. B and C each ignore one of the two hazards the handbook names.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the induction system should be kept clean at all times for exactly these reasons.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: The system should be kept clean at all times, since pieces of rags or paper can restrict the airflow if allowed to enter the air intakes or ducts. Loose bolts and nuts can cause serious damage if they pass into the engine.

notes.front: After a dirty oiled carburettor air filter element has been cleaned and dried, how is it usually treated before refitting?
notes.back: Immersed in a mixture of oil and rust-preventive compound, with the excess allowed to drain off.
notes.explanation: Paper-type filters are not cleaned this way: they are inspected and replaced as needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: After it has dried, it is usually immersed in a mixture of oil and rust-preventive compound. The excess fluid should be allowed to drain off before the filter element is reinstalled. Paper-type filters should be inspected and replaced as needed.

notes.front: An engine with an induction air filter will not start, and on another day it made low power. Which cause fits both symptoms?
notes.back: C) An excessively dirty induction air filter
notes.choices:
A) An alternate air valve stuck open
B) Carburettor heat left in the cold position
C) An excessively dirty induction air filter
D) A balance tube with no pressure imbalance
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: an open alternate air path lets air in rather than blocking it. B is the normal setting when there is no icing. D describes correct operation.
notes.explanation: The handbook says an excessively dirty filter causes a loss of power or stops the engine starting.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 3-4
notes.evidence: If the induction system air filter becomes excessively dirty, it will cause a loss of power or the engine will not start.

notes.front: An engine idles improperly. Inspection finds the intake pipe packing has shrunk and no longer fits. What remedy does the induction troubleshooting guide give?
notes.back: D) Replace the packing
notes.choices:
A) Clean the air filter
B) Tighten the air ducts only
C) Lubricate the engine valves
D) Replace the packing
notes.choicesExplained: A cures a dirty filter causing low power. B cures loose air ducts causing rough running. C cures sticking valves causing rough running.
notes.explanation: The guide lists shrunken intake packing, a hole in an intake pipe and loose carburettor mounting as causes of improper idling.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Induction System Troubleshooting”, p. 3-5
notes.evidence: Shrunken intake packing Inspect packing for proper fit Replace packing

notes.front: A radial engine’s compressor takes the air-fuel mixture leaving the carburettor and is geared to the crankshaft. How is this supercharging system classified?
notes.back: A) Internally driven
notes.choices:
A) Internally driven
B) Externally driven (turbocharger)
C) Normalising turbocharger
D) Ground-boosted turbocharger
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D are all exhaust-driven types, which compress air before it is mixed with fuel.
notes.explanation: Internally driven superchargers compress the mixture after the carburettor; turbochargers compress air before fuel is mixed in.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Supercharged Induction Systems”, p. 3-5
notes.evidence: Internally driven superchargers compress the air-fuel mixture after it leaves the carburetor, while externally driven superchargers (turbochargers) compress the air before it is mixed with the

notes.front: To be a true supercharger, a system must boost manifold pressure above {{c1::30 "Hg}}, that is, above ambient pressure.
notes.explanation: Normalising systems regain pressure lost with altitude but never boost above this figure, so they are not true superchargers.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Supercharged Induction Systems”, p. 3-5
notes.evidence: boost the manifold pressure above 30 inches of mercury. In other words, a true supercharger boosts the manifold pressure above ambient pressure.

notes.front: In an engine with an internally driven supercharger, what two temperature limits must the charge meet?
notes.back: Warm enough for complete fuel vaporisation and even distribution; not so hot that it cuts volumetric efficiency or causes detonation.
notes.explanation: Air gains heat as it is compressed, so these systems carry pressure- and temperature-sensing devices and units to warm or cool the air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Internally Driven Superchargers”, p. 3-6
notes.evidence: For example, the charge must be warm enough to ensure complete fuel vaporization and, thus, even distribution. At the same time, it must not be so hot that it reduces volumetric efficiency or causes detonation.

notes.front: A pilot reports that a light aircraft’s normalising turbocharger system gives no boost while cruising at 3,000 feet. What should the mechanic check first?
notes.back: D) The design operating altitude: many such systems operate only above a set altitude, 5,000 feet for example
notes.choices:
A) Whether the carburettor heat is on
B) Nothing: normalising systems never produce boost
C) Whether the manifold pressure should read above 30 "Hg at that height
D) The design operating altitude: many such systems operate only above a set altitude, 5,000 feet for example
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: they regain pressure lost with altitude. C is wrong: a normalising system never boosts above 30 "Hg. A has no bearing on turbocharger operation here.
notes.explanation: Below that altitude, maximum power is available without normalising, so no boost there may be normal.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Normalizer Turbocharger”, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: On many small aircraft engines, the turbocharger (normalizing) system is designed to be operated only above a certain altitude, 5,000 feet for example, since maximum power without normalizing is

notes.front: How does a ground-boosted turbocharger’s manifold pressure differ from a normalising system’s?
notes.back: Ground-boosted raises it above 30 "Hg, to around 40 "Hg; normalising never boosts above 30 "Hg.
notes.explanation: An engine must be boosted above 30 "Hg to be truly supercharged, which only the ground-boosted type does.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Ground-Boosted Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: As was mentioned earlier, an engine must be boosted above 30 "Hg to truly be supercharged. This type of turbocharger accomplishes this by increasing the manifold pressure above 30 "Hg to around 40 "Hg.

notes.front: Which main part of a turbosupercharger is made up of an impeller, a diffuser and a casing?
notes.back: The compressor assembly.
notes.explanation: Its diffuser vanes direct the air leaving the impeller and convert its high velocity to high pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbosuperchargers”, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: The compressor assembly is made up of an impeller, a diffuser, and a casing.

notes.front: Which main part of a turbosupercharger is driven by exhaust gases and drives the impeller?
notes.back: The turbine wheel (exhaust gas turbine) assembly.
notes.explanation: The turbo housing collects exhaust gases and directs them onto the turbine wheel, while the waste gate sets how much goes there.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbosuperchargers”, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: The turbine wheel, driven by exhaust gases, drives the impeller. The turbo housing collects and directs the exhaust gases onto the turbine wheel, and the waste gate regulates the amount of exhaust gases directed to the turbine.

notes.front: What is the third main part of a typical turbosupercharger, besides the compressor and turbine wheel assemblies?
notes.back: A full floating shaft bearing assembly.
notes.explanation: The rotor, the impeller and turbine on one shaft, revolves on oil-fed bearings supplied with engine oil.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbosuperchargers”, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: is composed of three main parts: 1. Compressor assembly, Ring type oil seal 2. Turbine wheel assembly, and Diffuser chamber 3. A full floating shaft bearing assembly.

notes.front: When a turbocharger’s waste gate is fully {{c1::open}}, nearly all the exhaust gases pass overboard, providing little or no boost.
notes.explanation: With the waste gate completely closed, all the exhaust gases are backed up and forced through the turbine wheel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbosuperchargers”, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: If the waste gate is completely closed, all the exhaust gases are “backed up” and forced through the turbine wheel.

notes.front: In most turbocharger systems, how does the controller make the waste gate close further?
notes.back: By restricting the engine oil flow, which raises oil pressure in the waste gate actuator.
notes.explanation: More closed means more exhaust through the turbine, a faster compressor and higher inlet pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Normalizer Turbocharger”, p. 3-10
notes.evidence: The more the oil is restricted, the more pressure is in the waste gate actuator and the more closed the waste gate is. This causes the exhaust gases to pass through the turbine, increasing the speed of the compressor raising the inlet pressure.

notes.front: A mechanic connects a gauge to the duct between the turbocharger compressor outlet and the throttle body. Which pressure will it show?
notes.back: C) Deck pressure (upper deck pressure)
notes.choices:
A) Manifold pressure
B) Engine oil pressure at the waste gate actuator
C) Deck pressure (upper deck pressure)
D) Ambient pressure at the ram-air intake
notes.choicesExplained: A is measured after the throttle, where the mixture enters the cylinders. B is oil, not induction air. D is upstream of the compressor.
notes.explanation: Turbocharger controllers sense this pressure to decide how far to close the waste gate.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Normalizer Turbocharger”, p. 3-10
notes.evidence: The pressure from the outlet of the compressor of the turbocharger to the throttle is referred to as deck pressure or upper deck pressure.

notes.front: In flight, the induction air filter of a ground-boosted turbocharged engine clogs. What keeps air flowing to the compressor?
notes.back: C) An alternate air door, opened automatically by compressor suction, admitting heated engine-compartment air
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the engine loses power until the filter is changed
B) The waste gate opens fully to bypass the filter
C) An alternate air door, opened automatically by compressor suction, admitting heated engine-compartment air
D) Carburettor heat is applied automatically
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the alternate air door. B is wrong: the waste gate controls exhaust, not induction air. D describes no feature of this system.
notes.explanation: In many cases the alternate air door can also be operated manually.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Ground-Boosted Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-9
notes.evidence: An alternate air door within the nacelle permits compressor suction automatically to admit alternate air (heated engine compartment air) if the induction air filter becomes clogged. In many cases, the alternate air door can be operated manually in the event of filter clogging.

notes.front: How does the waste gate position change as a turbocharged aircraft climbs at a constant manifold pressure setting?
notes.back: Almost fully open at sea level, it moves towards closed as the aircraft climbs.
notes.explanation: Once it is fully closed, further climb makes manifold pressure drop: critical altitude has been reached.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-12
notes.evidence: Thus, the waste gate is almost fully open at sea level and continues to move toward the closed position as the aircraft climbs, in order to maintain the preselected manifold pressure setting.

notes.front: A turbocharged aircraft cannot reach its published critical altitude. Which fault would explain this?
notes.back: A) The waste gate will not close fully
notes.choices:
A) The waste gate will not close fully
B) The waste gate will not open
C) The one-way oil check valve holds oil out of the turbocharger when stopped
D) The alternate air door is closed with a clean filter
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a waste gate stuck closed drives full exhaust through the turbine. C and D describe normal operation.
notes.explanation: The handbook states that an aircraft whose waste gate will not close fully cannot reach its critical altitude.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-12
notes.evidence: If a turbocharger waste gate will not close fully, then the aircraft will not be able to reach its critical altitude.

notes.front: In a sea level booster system, what does the density controller do?
notes.back: It limits manifold pressure below critical altitude, regulating bleed oil only at full throttle, using nitrogen-filled bellows.
notes.explanation: The bellows keep a constant density by allowing pressure to rise as temperature rises.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-13
notes.evidence: The density controller is designed to limit the manifold pressure below the turbocharger’s critical altitude and regulates bleed oil only at the full throttle position.

notes.front: In a sea level booster system, when does the differential pressure controller work?
notes.back: In all waste gate positions other than fully open, sensing pressure on both sides of the throttle.
notes.explanation: At part throttle the differential rises, so it bleeds oil and repositions the waste gate piston.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-13
notes.evidence: The differential pressure controller functions during all positions of the waste gate valve other than the fully open position, which is controlled by the density controller.

notes.front: How does bootstrapping differ from overboost?
notes.back: Bootstrapping is an unregulated drift of manifold pressure that does not harm engine life; overboost exceeds manifold pressure limits and can cause serious damage.
notes.explanation: The differential pressure controller reduces bootstrapping by shortening the time the system takes to reach equilibrium.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-14
notes.evidence: Bootstrapping is sometimes confused with the condition known as overboost, but bootstrapping is not a condition that is detrimental to engine life.

notes.front: A pilot of a turbocharged aircraft sets a manifold pressure after a quick throttle movement and finds it has changed a few seconds later. What does the handbook recommend?
notes.back: A) Make throttle changes slowly and wait a few seconds for the system to settle
notes.choices:
A) Make throttle changes slowly and wait a few seconds for the system to settle
B) Replace the density controller at once
C) Ground the aircraft: the drift is overboost
D) Readjust the waste gate linkage for more opening
notes.choicesExplained: B and D are wrong: overshoot is not a component fault. C is wrong: the handbook says overshoot is not a dangerous condition.
notes.explanation: This drift, called overshoot, happens because the automatic controls cannot respond fast enough to abrupt throttle changes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “A Typical Turbosupercharger System”, p. 3-14
notes.evidence: Since the automatic controls cannot respond rapidly enough to abrupt changes in throttle settings to eliminate the inertia of turbocharger speed changes, overshoot must be controlled by the operator. This can best be accomplished by slowly making changes in throttle setting, accompanied by a few seconds’ wait for the system to reach a new equilibrium.

notes.front: What does an unstable waste gate or controller cause in a turbocharged engine?
notes.back: The engine surges because of erratic manifold pressure.
notes.explanation: The controller senses deck pressure and controls oil flow through the waste gate actuator, so instability shows up as manifold pressure swings.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbocharger Controllers & System Descriptions”, p. 3-14
notes.evidence: If a malfunction occurs causing the waste gate or controller to not be stable, it will cause the engine to surge due to an erratic manifold pressure.

notes.front: On a hot day, a turbocharged engine’s compressor could deliver air far hotter than the 230–300 °F throttle inlet limits typical of reciprocating engines. Which component deals with this?
notes.back: C) An aftercooler (intercooler) between the compressor and the throttle inlet
notes.choices:
A) A closed waste gate
B) Carburettor heat, applied at take-off
C) An aftercooler (intercooler) between the compressor and the throttle inlet
D) Closed cowl flaps
notes.choicesExplained: B and A would add heat or boost, making the charge hotter. D reduces engine cooling airflow and does nothing for induction air.
notes.explanation: Compression can raise induction air temperature by a factor of five; the handbook gives this as the reason for cooling the compressed air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbocharger Controllers & System Descriptions”, p. 3-14
notes.evidence: Most turbochargers are capable of compressing the induction air to the point at which it can raise the air temperature by a factor of five.

notes.front: A turbocharger controller has an aneroid referenced to upper deck pressure, does nothing until a set absolute pressure is reached, and then bypasses oil. Which controller is it?
notes.back: A) An absolute pressure controller
notes.choices:
A) An absolute pressure controller
B) A variable absolute pressure controller
C) A differential pressure controller
D) A sloped controller
notes.choicesExplained: D also senses throttle differential and trims pressure at part throttle. B schedules its pressure with a throttle-driven cam. C works at all waste gate positions except fully open.
notes.explanation: It controls only the maximum compressor discharge pressure, and the system needs no pilot action up to critical altitude.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Absolute Pressure Controller”, p. 3-15
notes.evidence: As an absolute pressure setting is reached, it bypasses oil, and relieves the pressure on the waste gate actuator. This allows the absolute pressure controller to control the maximum turbocharger compressor discharge pressure.

notes.front: A turbocharged engine’s waste gate will not open. What probable causes does the handbook’s troubleshooting table list?
notes.back: An obstructed oil outlet, broken waste gate linkage, or a controller malfunction.
notes.explanation: With oil unable to return, pressure stays on the actuator; the remedy is to clean and reconnect the oil return line.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbocharger System Troubleshooting”, p. 3-16
notes.evidence: Oil outlet obstructed Clean and reconnect oil return line Broken wastegate linkage Replace linkage and adjust waste gate opening and closing Controller malfunction

image.alt: Table with three columns: trouble, probable cause, remedy. Fails to reach critical altitude: damaged compressor or turbine wheel, exhaust leaks, faulty bearings, waste gate not closing, controller fault. Engine surges: bootstrapping, waste gate or controller fault. Waste gate will not close fully: tight bypass valve bearing, blocked oil inlet orifice, differential controller fault, broken linkage. Waste gate will not open: obstructed oil outlet, broken linkage, controller fault. Differential controller: leaking seals, broken diaphragm, stuck valve. Density controller: leaking seals, damaged bellows, stuck valve; each controller fault is remedied by replacing the controller.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA-H-8083-32B, Chapter 3, Figure 3-23

notes.front: What does coke (carbon) building up inside the turbocharger itself cause?
notes.back: A gradual loss of power in flight and a low manifold pressure reading before take-off.
notes.explanation: The handbook says periodic de-coking has proved necessary to keep peak efficiency.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Exhaust Systems with Turbocharger”, p. 3-24
notes.evidence: Coke deposit buildup in the turbo itself causes a gradual loss of power in flight and low manifold pressure reading prior to takeoff. Experience has shown that periodic de-coking, or removal of carbon deposits, is necessary to maintain peak efficiency.

notes.front: On the Rotax 914, why should the throttle be moved smoothly through the 108–110 percent range?
notes.back: Nominal boost rises rapidly there, so small throttle changes have a big effect and can cause control fluctuations or surging.
notes.explanation: The throttle position sensor reads 0 to 115 percent from idle to full power.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Turbocharger & Control System”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: As shown in the diagram, with the throttle position at 108–110 percent results in a rapid rise of nominal boost pressure. To avoid unstable boost, the throttle should be moved smoothly through this area either to full power (115 percent) or at a reduced power setting to maximum continuous power.

notes.front: After switching on a Rotax 914’s supply, both TCU lamps light for one to two seconds and go out, and then the orange caution lamp starts blinking. What does this mean?
notes.back: C) The TCU or its periphery systems have malfunctioned
notes.choices:
A) The TCU is ready for operation
B) Full throttle has been held for more than 5 minutes
C) The TCU or its periphery systems have malfunctioned
D) The lamp test failed and must be repeated
notes.choicesExplained: A is signalled by the orange lamp staying out. B is signalled by the red boost lamp blinking. D: the lamp test passed, since both lamps lit and went out.
notes.explanation: A steadily unlit orange lamp signals the TCU is ready; blinking indicates a malfunction.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Turbocharger & Control System”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: If the orange caution lamp is not illuminated, then this signals that TCU is ready for operation. If the lamp is blinking, this indicates a malfunction of the TCU or its periphery systems.

notes.front: What are the three principal reasons excessive heat is undesirable in an internal-combustion engine?
notes.back: It affects combustion of the charge, weakens and shortens the life of parts, and impairs lubrication.
notes.explanation: Too hot a cylinder preheats the mixture so it burns early, causing detonation and knocking.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-32
notes.evidence: Excessive heat is undesirable in any internalcombustion engine for three principal reasons: 1. It affects the behavior of the combustion of the air-fuel charge. 2. It weakens and shortens the life of engine parts. 3. It impairs lubrication.

notes.front: In a typical aircraft powerplant, where does the heat released by burning fuel go?
notes.back: About one quarter becomes useful power; of the rest, half leaves with the exhaust and half is absorbed by the engine.
notes.explanation: Oil carries part of the absorbed heat to the oil cooler, and the cooling system takes the rest.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-32
notes.evidence: About one-fourth of the heat released is changed into useful power. The remainder of the heat must be dissipated so that it is not destructive to the engine. In a typical aircraft powerplant, half of the heat goes out with the exhaust and the other is absorbed by the engine.

notes.front: Why must an aircraft engine also be kept from running too cold?
notes.back: Fuel evaporation and distribution and oil circulation depend on the engine being at its optimum operating temperature.
notes.explanation: Without cooling controls, the engine could overheat on take-off and get too cold in high-speed, low-power descents.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-33
notes.evidence: Fuel evaporation and distribution and oil circulation depend on an engine being kept at its optimum operating temperature.

notes.front: A mechanic is about to ground-run an engine fitted with cowl flaps. How should the cowl flaps be set?
notes.back: C) Opened wide, since drag does not matter on the ground and cooling should be at maximum
notes.choices:
A) Closed, to warm the engine quickly
B) Opened just enough to stay below red line, as for take-off
C) Opened wide, since drag does not matter on the ground and cooling should be at maximum
D) Half open, whatever the engine temperature
notes.choicesExplained: A risks overheating: cooling should be at maximum on the ground. B is the take-off setting, chosen to limit drag. D ignores the handbook’s rule for ground operation.
notes.explanation: On take-off, by contrast, they are opened only enough to keep the engine below red line, to keep drag low.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-33
notes.evidence: On takeoff, the cowl flaps are opened only enough to keep the engine below the red-line temperature. Heating above the normal range is allowed so that drag is as low as possible. During ground operations, the cowl flaps should be opened wide since drag does not matter and cooling needs to be set at maximum.

notes.front: What happens to engine temperature when the cowl flaps are closed, and why?
notes.back: It tends to rise: closing them shrinks the exit area, so less air circulates over the cylinder fins.
notes.explanation: Opening them enlarges the exit area, increases cooling airflow and lets engine temperature fall.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling System Maintenance”, p. 6-34
notes.evidence: Closing the cowl flaps decreases the exit area, which effectively decreases the amount of air that can circulate over the cylinder fins. The decreased airflow cannot carry away as much heat; therefore, it has a tendency for the engine temperature to increase.

notes.front: What two functions does the engine cowling perform?
notes.back: It streamlines the engine to reduce drag, and forms an envelope that forces air around and between the cylinders.
notes.explanation: Inside that envelope the air absorbs the heat given off by the cylinder fins.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling System Maintenance”, p. 6-34
notes.evidence: The cowling performs two functions: 1. It streamlines the bulky engine to reduce drag. 2. It forms an envelope around

notes.front: An engine with complete cylinder head baffling runs hot. The rubber air seal on one cowl panel is found torn away. Why does this matter?
notes.back: B) Air can escape without being forced around and through the baffle system
notes.choices:
A) It does not: the seal only stops rain entering
B) Air can escape without being forced around and through the baffle system
C) It lets exhaust gas into the cabin
D) It jams the cowl flaps open
notes.choicesExplained: A and D give the seal a job the handbook does not describe. C confuses the cowl air seal with exhaust system seals.
notes.explanation: The seal must be used on such engines to force the air to circulate around and through the baffles.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Maintenance of Engine Cowling”, p. 6-36
notes.evidence: The engine air seal must be used on engines that have a complete cylinder baffling system that covers the cylinder heads. Its purpose is to force the air to circulate around and through the baffle system.

notes.front: For cooling fin inspection, fin area is the total area of {{c1::both sides}} of the fin exposed to the air.
notes.explanation: Fin area is what decides whether a cylinder with broken fins is accepted or removed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Engine Cylinder Cooling Fin Inspection”, p. 6-36
notes.evidence: Fin area is the total area (both sides of the fin) exposed to the air.

notes.front: What can be done about small cracks and rough corners on cylinder cooling fins?
notes.back: Small cracks can be filled or stop-drilled; rough or sharp corners can be smoothed by filing.
notes.explanation: Small cracks are not in themselves a reason to remove the cylinder, but reprofiling limits come from the manufacturer.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Engine Cylinder Cooling Fin Inspection”, p. 6-36
notes.evidence: Small cracks are not a Figure 6-56. A cylinder head and fins. reason for cylinder removal. These cracks can be filled or even sometimes stop-drilled to prevent any further cracking. Rough or sharp corners on fins can be smoothed out by filing

notes.front: On the handbook’s example engine, three adjacent cooling fins on one cylinder head are broken over a total length of five inches. What should be done?
notes.back: B) Remove and replace the cylinder, since the example allows four inches on any three adjacent fins
notes.choices:
A) Keep the cylinder in service: up to six inches is allowed on adjacent fins
B) Remove and replace the cylinder, since the example allows four inches on any three adjacent fins
C) Stop-drill the fins and return it to service
D) File the broken edges smooth and return it to service
notes.choicesExplained: A misreads the limit: six inches is for two adjacent fins. D and C are for small cracks and rough corners, not breakage over the limit.
notes.explanation: The limits (six inches on two adjacent fins, four on three, two on four, one on five) apply only to that engine; use the manufacturer’s figures.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Engine Cylinder Cooling Fin Inspection”, p. 6-36
notes.evidence: Where adjacent fins are broken in the same area, the total length of breakage permissible is six inches on any two adjacent fins, four inches on any three adjacent fins, two inches on any four adjacent fins, and one inch on any five adjacent fins.

notes.front: In pressure cooling, what forces the cooling air past the cylinders?
notes.back: The pressure difference between high pressure above the engine and low pressure at the cowl exit at the bottom rear.
notes.explanation: Air piles up at the top, slowing and raising pressure, and speeds up again as it nears the exit.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Baffle & Deflector System Inspection”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: The pressure differential between the top and the bottom of the engine forces the air past the cylinders through the passages formed by the deflectors.

notes.front: Why do baffles need an appreciable pressure differential across the engine, and what reduces the air volume required?
notes.back: Baffles resist the passage of cooling air; properly designed and located cylinder deflectors greatly reduce the volume needed.
notes.explanation: The air baffle stops air leaving the cylinder head and forces it between the head and the deflector.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Baffle & Deflector System Inspection”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: Although the resistance offered by baffles to the passage of the cooling air demands that an appreciable pressure differential be maintained across the engine to obtain the necessary airflow, the volume of cooling air required is greatly reduced by employing properly designed and located cylinder deflectors.

notes.front: With the cowling off for a spark plug change, a mechanic finds a crack just starting in a cylinder baffle and a small dent in a deflector. What does the handbook allow?
notes.back: B) Stop-drill the crack and straighten the dent, permitting further service
notes.choices:
A) Leave both until the next regular engine inspection
B) Stop-drill the crack and straighten the dent, permitting further service
C) Replace the cylinder, since baffle damage causes hot spots
D) Remove the baffle and deflector and fly without them
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: they should be checked whenever the cowling is off. C is wrong: the defect is in the baffle, not the cylinder. D would remove the parts that force air around the cylinder.
notes.explanation: Baffles and deflectors should be checked whenever the cowling is removed; only severe cracks or dents need repair or replacement.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Baffle & Deflector System Inspection”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: Cracks or dents, if severe enough, would necessitate repair or removal and replacement of these units. However, a crack that has just started can be stop-drilled, and dents can be straightened, permitting further service from these baffles and deflectors.

notes.front: On an aircraft with augmentor cooling, engine temperature falls too far during a descent from altitude. What can be done with the augmentor vanes?
notes.back: A) Close them, to prevent the engine cooling too much
notes.choices:
A) Close them, to prevent the engine cooling too much
B) Open the cowl flaps as well
C) Apply carburettor heat to warm the cylinders
D) Leave them in trail for maximum flow
notes.choicesExplained: D and B increase cooling airflow. C heats induction air, not the cylinders.
notes.explanation: They are usually left in trail for maximum flow; closing them also raises heat for cabin or anti-icing use.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 6-33
notes.evidence: These vanes are usually left in the trail position to permit maximum flow. They can be closed to increase the heat for cabin or anti-icing use or to prevent the engine from cooling too much during descent from altitude.

notes.front: In a cylinder temperature indicating system, what are the thermocouple’s dissimilar metals generally made of?
notes.back: Constantan and iron.
notes.explanation: A temperature difference between the junction and the wire connection produces a voltage that drives current to the indicator.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: The thermocouple consists of two dissimilar metals, generally constantan and iron, connected by wiring to an indicating system.

notes.front: While fitting a new CHT thermocouple, a mechanic finds the lead much too long for the installation. What should be done with the extra length?
notes.back: D) Coil and tie up the excess, since shortening the lead gives a wrong reading
notes.choices:
A) Cut it to length and re-terminate it
B) Cut it and recalibrate the indicator
C) Splice in a shorter copper lead
D) Coil and tie up the excess, since shortening the lead gives a wrong reading
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and B all change the lead the thermocouple was designed around, giving an incorrect reading.
notes.explanation: The thermocouple is designed to produce a given resistance, so cutting the lead changes the indicated temperature.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Cylinder Temperature Indicating Systems”, p. 6-37
notes.evidence: When installing a thermocouple lead, remember not to cut off the lead because it is too long, but coil and tie up the excess length. The thermocouple is designed to produce a given amount of resistance. If the length of the lead is reduced, an incorrect temperature reading results.

notes.front: What is the main problem with liquid cooling, and what does it allow?
notes.back: The added weight of coolant, radiator and tubing; it does allow high power to be obtained safely.
notes.explanation: Most reciprocating aircraft engines are air cooled, with liquid cooling used on a few high-powered engines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Engines, “Types of Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-3
notes.evidence: The main problem with liquid cooling is the added weight of coolant, heat exchanger (radiator), and tubing to connect the components. Liquid cooled engines do allow high power to be obtained from the engine safely.

notes.front: In a Rotax liquid cooling system, what happens to coolant as it heats and then cools?
notes.back: Heating opens the pressure cap’s excess pressure valve, sending coolant to the overflow bottle; cooling sucks it back into the circuit.
notes.explanation: The overflow bottle is transparent and the coolant reaches it at atmospheric pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Rotax 912/914: Cooling System”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: As the temperature of the coolant rises, the excess pressure valve opens and the coolant flows via a hose at atmospheric pressure to the transparent overflow bottle (4). When cooling down, the coolant is sucked back into the cooling circuit.

notes.front: How is the Rotax 582 two-stroke engine cooled?
notes.back: By liquid-cooled cylinders and cylinder heads in a two-circuit system, fed by an integrated pump.
notes.explanation: Unlike the air-cooled 447 and 503, the 582 sends coolant through the cylinders and heads to a radiator.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 11, Light-Sport Aircraft Engines, “Cooling System of the Rotax 582 UL DCDI”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: Engine cooling for the Rotax 582 is accomplished by liquid cooled cylinders and cylinder heads. [Figure 11-4] The cooling system is in a two circuit arrangement.

notes.front: Which Airman Certification Standards skill relates to the coolant of a liquid-cooled engine?
notes.back: Locating the proper specifications for the coolant used in a liquid-cooled engine.
notes.explanation: The standards also list chemicals used in liquid cooling systems as a risk to identify and mitigate.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (2021), Section III, Subject J, Reciprocating Engine Induction and Cooling Systems, p. 55
notes.evidence: AM.III.J.S10 Locate the proper specifications for coolant used in a liquid-cooled engine.
